Hi Laura,

Thanks again for taking this preflight. We're starting to assemble the hardware and would like Redwood's guidance on a couple of thorny items before we lock in the rack BOM: node sizing (CPU/GPU mix), NVMe placement for the model cache, and recommended persistent volume strategy for encrypted state.

Quick context: our cluster will host a mix of realtime low-latency endpoints (LLM inference) and batch embedding jobs. Target QPS for steady-state is ~300 req/s with bursts to 700 for 60–90s. Latency SLO is 150ms p50 for the realtime endpoints.

Two specific asks:
- Do you recommend local NVMe per inference node for prefix/KV cache, or a shared NVMe pool attached via NVMe-oF?
- For model artifacts and long-term state, should we rely on blockstore PVs (encrypted) or a hybrid approach with a small local model disk + remote blockstore for backups?

I'm attaching our rough site inventory (site-inventory-template.xlsx) and a first-pass network diagram.

Can we get a short call Friday to align on constraints and next actions?

Carlos —

Appreciate the details. Quick read of the inventory looks fine; a couple clarifying asks are inlined below. I pasted a short recommended preflight checklist and a proposed agenda for our Friday 30-minute sync.

On NVMe vs NVMe-oF
- Recommendation: local NVMe per inference node for KV/prefix cache. Rationale: reduces network jitter and preserves p50 latency for small token lookups. NVMe-oF can work for shared model stores but introduces tail volatility for sub-200ms SLOs unless you have guaranteed network fabric QoS (lossless, dedicated RDMA lanes).

On model artifacts / PV strategy
- Recommendation: hybrid. Keep a local encrypted model disk (fast NVMe, mounted read-only) for active model serving, and a remote encrypted blockstore for longer-term artifacts and backups. Use a small local persistent volume (e.g., LVM on NVMe) sized for the active model set and warm-start layers; sync to remote blockstore on a scheduled cadence + on rollout.

Node sizing (initial)
- Inference nodes: 8 x 80GB GPUs (or equivalent 4 x A40-style for cost) per rack for the initial 300–700 burst profile; 64 vCPU and 512GB RAM host is a good baseline for multi-GPU packing.
- Batch nodes: separate nodepool with no GPUs, higher CPU/RAM for embedding backfills (32vCPU/256GB).

Please: fill the attached inventory with precise NIC types and any ToR switch QoS capabilities. If possible, annotate whether the site can provide DCB/priority-based flow control for the RDMA fabric.

Proposed Friday agenda (30 mins)
1) Confirm NIC/ToR QoS and NVMe topology (5m)
2) Nodepool sizing and autoscaler knobs (10m)
3) PV encryption + backup cadence (5m)
4) Runbook handoff & next actions (10m)

I've attached our Redwood preflight checklist as a PDF and a short NVMe behavior note. If that works I'll send a calendar invite.

Laura Bennett
Customer Solutions Manager
Redwood Inference

Laura — forwarding a few low-level recommendations we should include in the invite and the runbook. I ran a quick microbenchmark on our NVMe caching profile; comments inline.

Key notes (summary):
- Local NVMe per inference node is the right default. If they insist on NVMe-oF, require dedicated RDMA fabric (lossless DCB) and per-tenant bandwidth policing to avoid noisy neighbor tail latency.
- For model warming: prefetch layer-wise weights into a read-only loopback mount on local NVMe prior to traffic ramp. That reduces cold-start spikes and keeps KV cache localized.
- Filesystem: ext4 with barrier support off for NVMe caching (we do writes rarely); use fsync control for rollout tooling.
- K8s PV patterns: use a CSI driver that supports volume cloning and snapshotting. Keep VL (Volume Lifecycle) policies: ephemeral model cache on local disk, PV claims for checkpoint/backups to remote blockstore.
- Autoscaler knobs: set scale-up cooldown to 10s for inference nodepool, but use predictive scheduled scale for known bursts.

Attached small nvme-benchmark.log (excerpt) — we saw 95th pct latency increase when a single flow saturated the fabric; this supports requiring QoS.

Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
